text: Tharparkar (Dhatki/Sindhi: ٿرپارڪر; Urdu: تھرپارکر, Urdu pronunciation: [t̪ʰəɾpɑːɾkəɾ]) is a district in Sindh province, Pakistan, with its headquarters in Mithi. Before Indian independence, it was known as the Thar and Parkar (1901–1947) or Eastern Sindh Frontier District (1860–1901). It is the largest district in Sindh and has the largest Hindu population in Pakistan, yet it holds the lowest Human Development Index rating among Sindh's districts. The Sindh government is currently planning to divide Tharparkar into Tharparkar and Chhachro districts. The name Tharparkar comes from a portmanteau of "Thar" (referring to the Thar Desert) and "parkar" (meaning "to cross over"). Historically, the Thar region was fertile, though it became mostly desertified between 2000 BCE and 1500 BCE; some historians speculate that a prehistoric river flowing through the area could be the ancient Sarasvati River mentioned in the Hindu Rigveda. The region is also referenced in the Ramayana as "Lavanasagara" (meaning "salt ocean"). After the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation, Sindh was ruled by dynasties including the Soomras, Sammas, Arghuns, Kalhoras, and Talpurs, who primarily governed central and western Sindh, with eastern areas like Tharparkar being neglected. In 1843, Charles James Napier defeated the Talpur dynasty and incorporated Tharparkar into the Cutch Agency and Hyderabad Collectorate. The British later divided Sindh into districts administered by British-appointed Zamindars. In 1858, the area became part of the Hyderabad District, and in 1860 it was established as the Eastern Sindh Frontier with headquarters at Amarkot. In 1882, it became a separate district with a Deputy Commissioner and political superintendent at Amarkot. In 1906, it was reorganized as the Thar and Parkar district, with its headquarters moved to Mirpur Khas. Prior to partition, Tharparkar had strong cultural and trading ties with Gujarat and Rajasthan, which persisted briefly afterward. During the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war, Indian forces captured large parts of Tharparkar in the Chachro Raid, but the area was returned to Pakistan after the Shimla Pact in 1972. On 31 October 1990, the district was divided into Tharparkar and Mirpur Khas, and on 17 April 1993, Umerkot was carved out of Tharparkar. Tharparkar lies between 69° 3′ 35″ E and 71° 7′ 47″ E longitude and 24° 9′ 35″ N and 25° 43′ 6″ N latitude. It borders Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Jalore in Rajasthan to the east, Kutch in Gujarat to the south, Umerkot to the north, and Badin and Mirpur Khas to the west. The district has a tropical semi-arid (Köppen: BSh) climate, with extremely hot days and cooler nights, hottest months in April, May, and June, and coldest in December, January, and February, with mean winter temperatures of 28 °C and 9 °C. Annual rainfall varies widely, with some areas receiving as little as 100 mm, and most precipitation occurring between July and September during the southwest monsoon. The highest recorded annual rainfall was 1306 mm in 2011. Tharparkar has suffered droughts since 1968, with official declarations in 1968, 1978, 1985, 1986, 1987, 1995, 1996, 1999, 2001, 2004, 2005, 2007, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2018. The region has at least 89 native plant species from 26 families, with herbs growing during the wet season and desert shrubs and drought-resistant trees year-round. The fauna is a significant cultural element, including the Chinkara Wildlife Sanctuary covering 940 km², where hunting and poaching are prohibited from Chelhar to Bhorelo and Mithi to Wajatto. Tharparkar is a major sanctuary for endangered vultures, and Gorano is a habitat for migratory birds. Peafowl conservation efforts aim to prevent further endangerment, and illegal exploitation of scorpions and snakes has been reported. The district is predominantly rural, with 96% of the population living outside urban areas. Agriculture is the primary economic activity, with livestock management as the main food source and economic base. Despite arid conditions, most Thari people are employed in farming; 1,014,000 hectares (50.4%) of the 2,011,000-hectare land are cultivated, with some areas using tube wells. 94% of households own livestock, and 77.64% of the population is engaged in livestock management. The average household owns 8 animals, with an estimated 7.7 million animals in total. Sheep are especially important, with 3 million kg of wool produced annually, and Tharparkar holds 40% of Sindh’s sheep population, considered the most suitable area for sheep in the province. 70.3% of farms use animals for plowing. Donkey numbers are notably high for an arid region. Despite the large livestock population, only 12 veterinarians serve the district. Art and artisanry, including ralli, pottery, puppet-making, carpet-making, block printing, cobbling, and embroidery, have long been part of Thari society. In Chachro taluka alone, there are 6,000 handlooms, providing economic opportunities, especially for women. Between 2002 and 2018, the district was represented in the Provincial Assembly by constituencies 60, 61, 62, and 63. In 2008, three of those seats were won by PML(Q) and one by PPP. In 2013, three PPP and one PML(N) candidates won. Before 2018, it was represented in the National Assembly by constituencies 229 and 230, both won by PML(Q) in 2008 and by PPP in 2013. After 2018 delimitation, it is represented in the Provincial Assembly by constituencies 54, 55, 56, and 57, and in the National Assembly by 221 and 222. In 2018, both national constituencies and three of the four provincial seats were won by PPP, with one provincial seat won by the Grand Democratic Alliance. Pakistan has 185.175 billion tonnes of lignite coal reserves, the seventh largest in the world, with Tharparkar holding 175.506 billion tonnes (95%) of those reserves, whose energy content exceeds that of Saudi Arabia and Iran combined. Power generation companies in Pakistan are exempt from income and turnover taxes, and imports for coal projects are tariff-exempt to encourage investment. Projects include a 600 MW project by the Chinese Shenhua Group and the 1200 MW Thar Engro Coal Power Project. Mineral mining is under provincial administration, but in 2011, the federal government created the Thar Coal & Energy Board (TCEB) to directly manage coal extraction. In March 2019, new members were appointed to TCEB, including female MNA Shazia Marri (NA-216), though the charter requires one female MNA from Tharparkar, Umerkot, or Mirpur Khas; an exception was made for MNA Mahesh Malani and Senator Krishna Kohli, both from the Thar region. The Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company supplies electricity to the national grid, yet most of the 2,300 registered and nearly 2,000 unregistered villages lack electricity. Energy shortages and blackouts are common, with a 22-hour heatwave outage resulting in deaths of hospital patients. A government announcement promised free electricity, but it has not been implemented, and supply continues through private companies like Hyderabad Electric Supply Company. Environmental and health concerns have been raised over coal mining, including habitat destruction, displacement, and increased risks of cancer, heart, and lung diseases. Social movements have emerged to address these issues. The Bahawalpur Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park has a PVOUT of 1596 kWh/kWp and GHI of 1925 kWh/m²/year, while Tharparkar has a PVOUT of 1642 kWh/kWp and GHI of 2005 kWh/m²/year. In January 2015, the largest solar reverse osmosis plant in Asia was completed in Mithi at a cost of US$2.98 million, filtering two million gallons daily, with smaller plants (10,000 gallons/day) installed at around US$24,900 each, funded by cooperation between the Sindh government and Pak Oasis. Despite these efforts, clean drinking water remains scarce, leading to illness and death. The efficacy and administration of these plants have been questioned, and in October 2018, workers went on strike after a four-month pay lapse, causing a water crisis. In July 2018, Pakistan’s National Accountability Bureau investigated allegations of an illegal contract award to Pak Oasis, including a premature payment of Rs 5 billion. In October 2018, the Sindh Chief Minister authorized Rs 336.7 million for 110 reverse osmosis plants, and in November 2018, the government decided to take over all RO plants in Thar Coal Block-II. On 16 April 2019, MPA Sidra Imran claimed in the Provincial Assembly that 700 solar reverse osmosis plants worth Rs 8 billion were not functional. Only 743 km of quality roads serve the 19,638 km² district, considered inadequate by NGOs. Major cities are connected by a highway, and talukas are linked to Mithi via metal roads. The Civil Aviation Authority of Pakistan built an airport in Islamkot at a cost of around Rs 972.07 million, covering 1,000 acres with a 3 km runway, serving both civilian and military traffic. The Sindh Coal Authority requested the airport, which is within 80 km of Pakistan’s India border, and received clearance from the Ministry of Defence on 25 September 2009. It was inaugurated on 17 July 2017 as Thar Airport and again on 11 April 2018 as Mai Bakhtawar Airport by Bilawal Bhutto Zardari. However, the PCAA does not recognize the airport, and it lacks an official website, ICAO, or IATA code. Before 1947, the Sind Mail ran between Hyderabad and Ahmedabad via Mirpur Khas, Khokhropar, Munabao, Barmer, Luni, Jodhpur, Pali, Marwar, and Palanpur. After partition, service continued with Khokhropar as the last station in Pakistan, used for customs, until it was halted after the 1965 war. Khokhropar and the Nagarparkar salient were captured by India in 1971 and returned in 1972. On 18 February 2006, after a 41-year suspension, service on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line resumed after track conversion to broad gauge. The newly built Zero Point railway station near Khokhropar is now the last station in Pakistan on this line and is used for customs enforcement. The Thar Express, a weekly train between Karachi and Jodhpur operated jointly by Pakistan and Indian Railways, covers 700 km in 32 hours and is nicknamed the 'torture train'.

After the partition of India in 1947, railway service continued on the line, with Khokhropar railway station, the last station in Pakistan on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line, used for customs. However, service was halted after the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965. During the 1971 war, the town of Khokhropar and the Nagarparkar salient were captured by India but were returned to Pakistan in 1972. On 18 February 2006, after a 41-year suspension, service on the Hyderabad–Jodhpur line resumed following the conversion of metre gauge track to broad gauge. The newly constructed Zero Point railway station near Khokhropar in Dahli taluka is now the last station in Pakistan on this line and is used for customs enforcement. The Thar Express, a weekly train operated jointly by Pakistan Railways and Indian Railways between Karachi and Jodhpur, covers a 700 km route that takes 32 hours, earning the nickname 'torture train' from some passengers. Despite formal petitions from Thari communities for rail service to support migration during droughts, government focus remains on improving coal mining infrastructure. In March 2009, the Pakistani Ministry of Information Technology’s Universal Service Fund awarded a Rs 930 million contract to Telenor Pakistan to build basic telephone and data infrastructure in Tharparkar. In March 2017, Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company, in partnership with Wateen Telecom, introduced free Wi-Fi to two villages—Tharyo Halepoto and Senhri Dars near Islamkot—providing 3 Mbit/s internet service at no cost, as the first stage of a larger initiative aimed at extending the service to all schools in Thar Coal Block II, with future phases targeting the entire block. Questions have been raised about the benefits of free Wi-Fi in a district where 87% of the population lives in absolute poverty. Paid telecommunications in Tharparkar are dominated by Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL), which holds a monopoly in the country. Access to drinking water is very limited, with only 47% of the population having access; 60% of households wait over an hour at wells, and 30% spend more than Rs 30 for two buckets of water. 85% of households use Pakhaal (rubber bags carried by camels or donkeys), while 25% use buckets carried by animals; in some areas, water collection takes up to two days, and 75% of women travel an average of 3 km per trip, spending 52% of their working hours fetching water. Basic waste management exists in urban areas, but rural areas—home to 96% of the district’s population—lack such facilities; 44% of households have no toilets, the highest rate in Sindh. Despite being a major source of Pakistan’s energy through its coal reserves, only 39% of Thari households use electricity as their primary lighting source, the lowest in Sindh. The district is mostly arid, with only 1.6% of cultivated land irrigated, mainly in Diplo taluka via a tributary of the Naukot branch of the Nara Canal; irrigation is more extensive in Nagarparkar and Mithi, where tube wells are used. 99% of households rely on firewood for cooking, with deforestation from large-scale harvesting potentially contributing to drought; 0.7% use gas, mostly in smaller urban areas, where gas infrastructure is underdeveloped and safety is questionable, with a common practice being the use of heavy objects on faulty valves to prevent leaks. Tharparkar’s economic importance stems from its coal reserves and status as Pakistan’s energy capital; during the September 2019 Pakistan Renewable Energy Summit, President Arif Alvi emphasized the need to fully utilize Thar’s coal reserves. The Sindh government called for increased Australian investment and auctioned off four coal mining blocks valued between US$4–6 billion. Chinese investment includes a US$2 billion contribution from Shanghai Electric Power Company Limited; as of November 2019, Pakistan and China agreed to expand the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor to include copper, gold, oil, gas, and housing. In 2019, the Asian Development Bank approved a $75 million loan for Sindhi education, and the World Bank approved a $1.93 billion loan for Sindh, including rural development in Tharparkar, though the timing—just after the Sindh CM was summoned by the National Accountability Bureau—has raised concerns about possible misuse of funds. Industrial investments have been promoted with economic incentives, but serious issues of industrial slave labor and worker exploitation persist. Domestic banking in Tharparkar is interest-free due to Islamization, though foreign currency loans and deposits incur interest; most banks are located in urban centers like Mithi and are closed on weekends; online banking is limited. All personal and corporate income is taxed federally except agricultural income, which is collected by the provincial government via the Board of Revenue (BOR). Under the Sindh Agricultural Income Tax Act of 2000, no land tax is levied in Thar Desert and Kohistan areas; an amendment bill passed by the Provincial Assembly on 30 April 2018 and formally notified on 22 May 2018 removed land tax. The Sindh cabinet also amended the Sindh Arms Act to allow individuals to keep more than four weapons; asset statements from legislators and senators in 2018 revealed high personal weapon holdings, and the Home Secretary was summoned over a fake arms license case. In November, reports indicated the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) would be restructured and the Prime Minister proposed replacing it. As of the 2023 census, Tharparkar has 327,584 households and a population of 1,778,407, with a sex ratio of 109.21 males per 100 females and a literacy rate of 36.39% (48.50% for males, 23.49% for females); 689,148 (38.76%) are under 10 years of age, and 144,405 (8.12%) live in urban areas. Before partition, Hindus and Muslims made up roughly 52% and 47% of the population, respectively; after partition, many Hindus emigrated to India, and about 3,500 Muslim families moved to Tharparkar from India, each receiving 12 acres (totaling 42,000 acres). After the 1965 and 1971 wars, many Hindus left Pakistan due to abuse in Chhachro and migrated to India. In the 1998 census, 59.42% were Muslim and 40.47% Hindu; by 2017, Muslims were 56.56% and Hindus 43.39%, with Hindus making up 64% of urban areas and Muslims 58% of rural areas—Tharparkar has the largest Hindu population in Pakistan. The northern taluks of Dahli, Chachro, Diplo, and Kaloi are majority Muslim, with Dahli nearly 90% Muslim; southern taluks of Islamkot, Mithi, and Nagarparkar are Hindu-majority, with Mithi nearly 70% Hindu. Most Hindus, especially in rural areas, are from lower castes and are Scheduled Castes, who constitute 28.05% of the district’s population, though this may be an underestimate as many Scheduled Castes report their religion as 'Hindu' rather than Scheduled Caste. The 2023 census recorded 99.36% of the population identifying as Sindhi, though Tharparkar is a linguistic transition zone between Sindhi, Rajasthani, and Gujarati, with Dhatki—the most widely spoken dialect—being closely related to Marwari and transitioning to Sindhi in the west; other languages include Koli dialects such as Parkari and Kachi Koli spoken near the Gujarat border. Tharparkar’s Human Development Index (HDI) is 0.227, ranking 109th out of 114 districts in Pakistan’s 2017 report—down from 103rd in 2013 and the lowest in Sindh—and it ranked among the ten worst districts for HDI growth between 2005 and 2015. The UNDP’s Multidimensional Poverty Index reports that 87% of Tharparkar’s population lives in poverty. Due to poor conditions, including low HDI and high infant mortality, a monitoring commission was established to oversee Sindh’s administration. The Benazir Income Support Programme and the World Food Programme agreed to reduce food insecurity; in 2019, Pakistan received US$362,000 and 4,727 metric tons of food aid. Humanitarian efforts included providing 50 kg of wheat 12 times to 287,000 families, constructing 500 small-scale water plants at a cost of Rs 7.5 billion, and planning a 250-bed hospital by the Thar Foundation (a joint venture of Sindh government and Engro) at a cost of Rs 2 billion, with the first 82-bed block completed in February 2019. Despite these efforts, infant mortality remains high, with around 1,500 children dying annually; between January and October 2019, 84 infants died, and in total, 703 children died; in 2016, the National Commission for Human Rights directed the Sindh Chief Secretary to submit a report on infant mortality. Sindh’s minister for Local Government, Public Health Engineering and Rural Development, Saeed Ghani, and Katchi Abadies introduced a mobile app to assist with wheat distribution, though no such app was developed and the system continues to rely on XLS/PDF files and web resources not widely distributed. According to legislator Mahesh Kumar Malani, Rs 15 billion has been spent on development projects in nine years, with further plans worth Rs 18 billion underway; the Chief Minister of Sindh stated that Rs 70 billion has been spent on infrastructure, and the Benazir Income Support Programme has transferred Rs 387 billion since 2008. Despite these efforts, the living standard index of Tharparkar fell by 50% between 2005 and 2015. Tharparkar has faced drought for at least 17 years and has been the focus of numerous NGO efforts, including USAID, DFID, and UN agencies, but no detailed statistical report on water resources or improvement measures has been published by the government. Thari people face challenges due to waterborne diseases, inadequate health facilities, famine, and lack of basic infrastructure. As of 2014, there were 140 health facilities in the district, including a district hospital with 50 beds and three tehsil hospitals with 80 beds each; these facilities met only 54% of the population’s needs in terms of healthcare and only 6% in terms of bedding. On average, 85% of births occur at home, with 56% in urban and 87% in rural areas; Tharparkar has the lowest rate of skilled birth attendance in Sindh, with only 16% of deliveries assisted by skilled personnel. Only about 25% of pregnant women receive tetanus toxoid injections (25% in rural areas, 37% in urban areas), and only 21% of infants aged 12–23 receive full immunization (32% in urban areas, 20% in rural areas). From 2011 to 2016, Sindh increased education spending by 90%, from PKR 14.26 billion to PKR 148 billion. Despite this, Tharparkar’s education situation remains poor: the overall literacy rate for those over 10 is 46%, with male literacy at 65% and female at 25%; urban areas have higher rates (69% overall, 81% male, 54% female), while rural areas have lower rates (45% overall, 64% male, 23% female); 37% of those over 15 are literate. The gross enrolment ratio (GER) for primary education is 84% (96% male, 71% female); urban GER is 105% (118% male, 92% female), significantly higher than the rural GER of 84% (95% male, 70% female). The net enrolment rate (NER) for primary education is not specified.

Spending in Tharparkar has increased by 90%, from PKR 14.26 billion to PKR 148 billion. Despite this rise in provincial expenditures, the district's educational situation remains poor. The overall literacy rate for people older than 10 is 46%, with male literacy at 65% and female literacy at 25%. Urban areas have higher literacy rates—averaging 69% (male: 81%, female: 54%)—while rural areas have lower rates—averaging 45% (male: 64%, female: 23%). Approximately 37% of those older than 15 are literate. The gross enrolment ratio (GER) for primary schooling is 84% (male: 96%, female: 71%), with urban GER at 105% (male: 118%, female: 92%) compared to rural GER at 84% (male: 95%, female: 70%). The net enrolment rate (NER) for primary schooling is 52% (male: 57%, female: 47%), with urban NER at 77% (male: 78%, female: 76%) and rural NER at 52% (male: 56%, female: 46%). A total of 221,203 students—125,189 male and 96,014 female—are enrolled in the district’s 4,152 schools, of which 620 are male-only, 629 are female-only, and 2,903 are co-ed. There are 5,469 teachers in total—4,813 male and 656 female—with an average of 53 students and 1.3 teachers per school, resulting in a student–teacher ratio of about 40, consistent across most levels. The Sindh Bureau of Statistics reports 4,010 schools in Tharparkar, the highest in Sindh. About 4.4% of schools have electricity, 34.6% have washrooms, 16.0% have drinking water, 0.4% have libraries, 0.6% have laboratories, and 2.2% have playgrounds. Approximately 74.5% of schools have school management committees. In April 2019, a social media movement using the hashtag #TharNeedsUniversity protested the lack of a university in Tharparkar, prompting the government to establish a sub-campus in Islamkot. NED University of Engineering and Technology, in partnership with Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company (SECMC) and The Citizens Foundation (TCF), announced the creation of the "Thar Institute of Engineering, Science, and Technology" as a sub-campus of NED, with an undergraduate program planned to start in October 2019, initially taught at the TCF-Engro Campus in Islamkot. However, after the Sindh government purchased 317 acres of land in Mithi for Rs 1.5 billion, the campus location was moved to the Benazir Cultural Complex in Mithi, following a payment of Rs 120 million. The temporary NED campus was inaugurated in October 2019 at the Shaheed Benazir Cultural Complex in Mithi, after the planned date for the cancelled Islamkot campus. Tharparkar is considered the most peaceful place in Pakistan, known for centuries-old interfaith harmony. Muslim residents do not sacrifice cows to avoid offending the Hindu community, while Hindu residents avoid celebrations during Muharram. Hindus fast and offer Iftar to Muslim neighbors during Ramadan, and both communities exchange sweets on Eid and Diwali. Muslims also refrain from eating meat during Navratri. There are no recorded instances of communal violence in the district. Thari people are predominantly vegetarian, with Singhri, Kair, and Guar being popular dishes. Key festivals include Teejdi, celebrated on Tritiya-Krishna Paksha of Bhadrapada, where married women fast for their husbands’ health and unmarried women pray for marital bliss; Thadri, celebrated one tithi before Krishna Janmasthmi, involving cold and probiotic foods like yogurt and pickle as a tribute to Sheetla Mata; Cheti Chand, marking the beginning of the Sindhi Hindu New Year on the first day of Chet (Chaitra); and Naurata, a nine-night festival of fasting and abstinence in honor of Durga, during which devotees offer meals and kheer to nine young girls and perform garba dances, with Ramlila and Ravana Dahan on Dussehra. Diyari, a five-day festival of lights beginning 18 days after Dussehra, includes Gau Puja, Shringar, Lakshmi Pujan, home cleaning, and illumination with diyas, and is considered auspicious for new beginnings, with political events often organized during this time, including a non-Hindu politician referencing Ravana in 2015 and nationwide anti-government marches in 2019. Major tourist destinations include 14 Jain temples and Bhodesar Mosque in Nagarparkar, inscribed on the tentative UNESCO World Heritage list as the Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape; Parbrahm Ashram (also known as Verijhap Dham or Chhari Saheb Dham) near Diplo, a Shiva temple visited annually during the "Parbrahma Jo Melo"; Gadi Bhit, the highest point in Mithi offering panoramic views; Churrio Jabal, a historic Durga Mata Temple visited annually by 200,000 pilgrims from Nepal, India, and other countries on Shivratri, with the hill mined for granite threatening the temple; Marvi Jo Khoh, a heritage well near Bhalva; and Sant Nenuram Ashram in Islamkot, which daily serves Bhandhara meals to all, feeds large numbers of birds, and hosts an annual three-day Sant Jo Melo festival in the Ashwina month. Karoonjhar Mountains, located near Nagarparkar, are about 19 km long and 305 meters high. Tharparkar is divided into 7 Tehsils, 64 Union Councils, 172 Dehs, and 2,365 villages. The district faces recurring challenges including drought, malnutrition, child mortality, suicide, and locust attacks, with drought declared in the district for at least 17 years before 2018. It is affected by earthquakes, floods, thunderstorms, drought, and locust attacks, with Nagarparkar particularly vulnerable. Climate change exacerbates existing environmental issues. Earthquakes occurred on 18 November and 1 December 2019, the latter during Sindhi Cultural Day celebrations. From May 2019 onward, large locust swarms destroyed crops, severely impacting agriculture and livelihoods. Activists criticized the government’s response, and in one incident, Agriculture Minister Ismail Rahoo suggested that the largely vegetarian population eat the insects as a solution. Farmers continued to labor to drive away locusts, with many crops destroyed, and demanded anti-insect spray. In October 2019, the government launched the "Ehsaas Langar Scheme" to provide free meals to needy families. An anti-government rally on 23 October was disrupted by locust swarms. Climate change also leads to severe thunderstorms and lightning strikes, killing over 30 people and livestock in November 2015 and nine people and many livestock in November 2019. Around 1.65 million people in Tharparkar live in homes without legal entitlement, with no city survey since 2014. Suicides are common, with 59 deaths—including 38 women and two children—in 2019 and about 198 in 2018, linked to increasing poverty and displacement. Many NGOs operate in the district for humanitarian aid, but in 2019, Pakistan cancelled the registration of 4,693 NGOs across Sindh, including 59 in Tharparkar, for violating regulations. Peafowls are culturally significant in Tharparkar, considered part of identity and heritage, commonly seen roaming rooftops, and historically noted for capturing the attention of Alexander the Great, who sent them to his mother. Peafowls are featured in pottery, rallis, and art, and are central to Sindhi folk songs like "Mor Tho Tilley Rana." Tharparkar cattle, known as White or Gray Sindhi, Cutchi, or Thari, are a dual-purpose breed recognized for both milking and draught potential, with milk production of approximately 1135 kg per lactation when kept on arid pasture, and lower when maintained in villages.

Peafowl holds a significant place in the cultural heritage of Tharparkar, frequently featured in the works of artists, poets, and singers from the region, exemplified by the Sindhi folk song "Mor Tho Tilley Rana." Tharparkar cattle, originating in the Tharparkar district, is a dual-purpose breed known as White or Gray Sindhi, Cutchi, and Thari, recognized for both milking and draught capabilities. During the first World War, these animals gained prominence when they were deployed to supply milk to Near East army camps, demonstrating their ability to produce milk under harsh feeding and environmental conditions. Reports indicate that Tharparkar cattle on arid pasture yield approximately 1135 kg of milk per lactation, while those in village settings average 1980 kg. Ralli, traditional quilts made by women in the Indus Region, derive their name from the local word "ralanna," meaning to mix or connect, and have been practiced since the 4th millennium BC. Historical trade records from the early 1500s list Ralli as an export item to Europe. The tradition has been passed down from mother to daughter for thousands of years, with women from all castes, religions, occupations, and tribes participating, many of whom are from underprivileged and poor backgrounds and view Ralli as a vital source of income. Women invest over 170 hours in creating each Ralli, which historically functioned as a form of textile currency in the ancient Indus Valley Civilization. In Tharparkar, Ralli quilts with peacock designs are especially popular. Kekra trucks, also known as Chakra by locals, are widely used for local transportation in Tharparkar due to their suitability for sandy terrain, earning them the nickname 'Camel of Thar.' These trucks are decorated with various designs and flowers and utilize powerful Bedford engines from World War II, contributing to their current popularity. Before road construction, people transported livestock and household goods via Kekra; today, they primarily carry goods and general items. Modifications to the chassis have increased their loading capacity, with a typical Kekra truck having a capacity of 12,000 kg. The practice of using traditionally decorated Kekra trucks has become a customary form of transportation in the Tharparkar district.
